hook.line: In a café, things slip, break and run out all day. Spanish has a neat way to say it happened to you without saying you did it, which is exactly what you want when a cup lands on the floor.
hook.es: Se me cayó tu taza. No fue mi intención.
hook.en: I dropped your cup. I didn't mean to.

examples.en: Did you drop something? (to a friend)

examples.es: A Vale se le cayó la bandeja.
Se me cayó la botella. No tiene importancia.
examples.en: I dropped the bottle. It doesn't matter.

rule:
English says *I dropped my phone*, as if you did something. Spanish often says the phone fell, and it happened to you.

*Se me cayó el celular.*

The thing is the subject, so the verb matches the thing:
*Se me cayó la botella.* (one)
*Se me cayeron las llaves.* (more than one)

The little word after *se* says who it happened to:
*me*, *te*, *le*, *nos*, *les*

The verb never changes for that person. To name them, put *a* in front: *A Vale se le cayó la bandeja.*

Use it for slips and accidents: dropping, forgetting, breaking, running out. If you did it on purpose, use the normal verb: *Tiré el vaso.*
smallPrint: Teachers call this the accidental or unplanned *se*. Colombians use it constantly.

options: You dropped your phone. (to a friend)
You forgot your key. (to a friend)
You forgot your keys. (to a friend)
You forgot to call me. (to a friend)
She forgot to call you. (to a friend)
I forgot to call you. (to a friend)
You dropped some bottles. (to a friend)

readAndPick.es: A Tomás se le rompió el vaso.

options: Your time ran out. (to a friend)

yourTurn.prompt: Fill the gap and type the whole sentence: Se me ___ el celular. (cayó / cayeron) I dropped my phone.
yourTurn.why: One phone, so the verb is the singular *cayó*.

yourTurn.prompt: Fill the gap and type the whole sentence: Se me ___ las llaves. (olvidó / olvidaron) I forgot my keys.
yourTurn.why: The keys are the subject and there is more than one, so *olvidaron*.
*Nos* is for us, and the verb matches the one thing, *el café*.

yourTurn.answer: A Vale se le cayó la bandeja.
accept: Se le cayó la bandeja a Vale.
yourTurn.why: *Le* says it happened to her, and *a Vale* tells us who.

yourTurn.prompt: Say to a friend: Did you drop something?
yourTurn.why: *Te* is for the person you are talking to.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about a friend (tú): Se me cayó el vaso.
yourTurn.why: Only the small word changes, from *me* to *te*. The verb stays.

yourTurn.prompt: Make the thing plural: Se me cayó la botella.
yourTurn.why: Two or more bottles, so the verb is *cayeron*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: Se me olvidó la llave.
yourTurn.answer: No se me olvidó la llave.

pitfalls.why: Almost. *Me caí* means *I fell*. When you drop something, the thing falls and it happens to you.
The verb matches the thing, not you. One phone, one *cayó*.
Close. The keys are the subject, and there is more than one, so *olvidaron*.
The verb never agrees with *me*. It agrees with *la llave*.

personal: Think of the last thing that slipped, broke or ran out on you. Write two lines with *se me*, *se nos* or *se le*, like *Se me acabó la leche.*
